questions.q: What does a rate limiter actually do for an API under heavy load?
questions.explain: A limiter refuses the excess from greedy or broken clients cheaply, protecting everyone else. Capacity itself comes from the database, instances and code efficiency.
options: Makes each request faster
Adds database capacity
Decides who gets the capacity that exists, so one client cannot use it all
Queues every request until the server is free

questions.q: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. What is the most a client can get through in about two seconds?
questions.explain: Each window counts on its own. Straddling a boundary doubles the burst. Sliding windows and token buckets do not have this edge.
options: 200: 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next
Unlimited

questions.q: What is the main cost of the sliding window log?
questions.explain: Exactness comes from remembering every recent request. For small limits that is fine; for large limits across millions of keys, the memory adds up, which is why the sliding counter exists.
options: It allows twice the limit at boundaries
It stores a timestamp for every allowed request, up to limit per key
It needs a timer per key
It cannot compute Retry-After

questions.q: A sliding window counter with a 60-second window is 15 seconds into the current window. How does it estimate the last 60 seconds?
questions.explain: The last 60 seconds contain 15 seconds of the current window and the last 45 seconds of the previous one. Assuming the previous window's requests were spread evenly, 45/60 of them are still inside.
options: current only
previous + current
previous × 45/60 + current
previous × 15/60 + current
It reads every timestamp from the last minute

questions.q: A token bucket has capacity 20 and refills 5 tokens per second. What do the two numbers control?
questions.explain: A full bucket lets 20 requests through at once. After that, the client can only sustain 5 per second, the rate at which tokens come back.
options: Capacity: requests per second; refill: the burst size
Capacity: the largest burst after a quiet period; refill: the long-run average rate
Both control the same thing in different units
Capacity: the number of clients; refill: the number of servers

questions.q: Why does a token bucket store "tokens and last update time" instead of using a timer to add tokens?
questions.explain: Lazy refill: tokens now = min(capacity, stored + elapsed × rate). No background work, and idle keys cost nothing but their stored numbers.
options: Timers are not allowed in Node.js servers
It can compute the refill when the next request arrives, so a million keys need no timers at all
It makes the bucket refill faster
So the bucket can hold negative tokens

questions.q: How does a leaky bucket differ from a token bucket?
questions.explain: A leaky bucket smooths output, useful in front of a slow downstream system. Public APIs usually prefer refusing quickly with 429 over making clients wait in a queue.
options: It refuses bursts larger than the capacity faster
It queues requests and releases them at a fixed rate, smoothing traffic instead of refusing it
It uses fixed windows internally
It is the same algorithm with a different name

questions.q: Which algorithm best fits "at most 5 log-in attempts per account per 15 minutes"?
questions.explain: With a fixed window an attacker could make 10 attempts around a boundary. The exact sliding log costs only a few timestamps per account here.
options: Fixed window, because it is simplest
Sliding log: the limit is small, strictness matters, and 5 timestamps per key is cheap
Token bucket with capacity 1000
No limit; account lockout is enough

questions.q: Opening your web app's dashboard fires 8 API requests at once, then nothing for a minute. Which limiter suits this traffic?
questions.explain: Normal use is bursty. A token bucket allows the burst and still caps the long-run rate, so real users are never refused while a script hammering the API is.
options: A token bucket with a capacity above 8 and a modest refill rate
A fixed window of 1 request per second
A sliding log of 2 per 10 seconds
A leaky bucket that releases 1 request per second

questions.q: Why can a strict per-IP limit hurt legitimate users?
questions.explain: Network address translation puts many devices behind one address. Keep per-IP limits generous and use per-user limits for fairness.
options: IP addresses change every request
Many users can share one public IP (an office, a university, a mobile network behind NAT) and then share one allowance
IPv4 addresses are too short to use as keys
Per-IP limits only work with HTTPS

questions.q: An API limits requests per API key, checked before verifying that the key exists. What does an attacker do?
questions.explain: Keys the attacker controls cannot be limit keys. Verify the key first, and count requests with unknown keys against the IP address.
options: Nothing; the limit stops them
Send a different made-up key on every request, so each gets a fresh allowance
Use a stolen real key
Send requests without any key

questions.q: Your API runs behind your own load balancer, which appends the client's address to X-Forwarded-For. Which entry should the limiter use?
questions.explain: Anyone can send an X-Forwarded-For header with any content, so the left-most values are client-controlled. Only entries added by proxies you run can be trusted. remoteAddress would be the load balancer itself.
options: The first (left-most) entry
The entry added by your own load balancer (the right-most one it appended), ignoring what the client wrote before it
A random entry
req.socket.remoteAddress, always

questions.q: Why do limiters often key IPv6 clients by their /64 prefix?
questions.explain: A /64 contains 264 addresses. Limiting per full address would let one client rotate through them freely.
options: IPv6 addresses cannot be stored as strings
One customer usually controls a whole /64 block and could use a new address for every request
The /64 prefix identifies the country
Browsers hide the last 64 bits

questions.q: A limiter computes that the client must wait 2.4 seconds. What should Retry-After say?
questions.explain: Retry-After is a whole number of seconds. Rounding down tells the client to come back too early, when it will be refused again. Always round up.

questions.q: Where in the request path should a per-IP limiter run?
questions.explain: A refusal must be cheaper than the work it prevents. Anything expensive done before the check is done for the attacker, too.
options: After the database transaction, so only successful requests count
After parsing and validating the JSON body
First, before authentication lookups, body parsing and any database work
In the client application

questions.q: A token bucket charges POST /transfers 5 tokens and GET /rates 1 token. Why?
questions.explain: Weighted costs make the limit track real load. One allowance covers both, and a client doing expensive work reaches the limit sooner.
options: POST requests are more likely to be attacks
A transfer costs the server far more than a cached read, so it should use more of the client's allowance
HTTP requires it
So GET requests are never refused

questions.q: A limit of 5 log-in attempts per 15 minutes is kept in memory, and the API runs as 4 instances behind a round-robin load balancer. How many attempts can an attacker make?
questions.explain: In-memory counts are per process. Security limits need a shared store with an atomic increment, such as a database row or Redis.
options: Up to 20: each instance counts its own 5
Unlimited

questions.q: Two instances share a counter. Each does SELECT count, adds one in JavaScript, then UPDATE. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: Read-then-write has a gap. Use one atomic statement, such as INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE SET count = count + 1 RETURNING count, or Redis INCR.
options: Nothing, the database is shared
Both read the same count, both write count + 1, and one increment is lost, so the limit is exceeded
The counter goes negative
The second UPDATE throws an error

questions.q: The Redis that stores rate limits is unreachable. What is a sensible policy?
questions.explain: A limiter outage should not take the whole API down, but it must not open an unlimited password-guessing window either. The choice is per limit, and it must be visible in monitoring.
options: Fail closed for everything: refuse all requests
Fail open for everything: allow all requests silently
Fail open for general API limits, fail closed for security limits such as log-in attempts, and alert either way
Restart the API until Redis is back

questions.q: An API gets 50,000 transfer requests per second. The database pool has 100 connections and each transfer holds one for 5 ms. What does a rate limiter change?
questions.explain: 100 / 0.005 s = 20,000 per second at best. A global limit below the ceiling keeps the database responsive; the excess gets a fast 429 or 503 with Retry-After instead of a slow timeout.
options: It lets all 50,000 transfers per second succeed
Nothing about capacity (at most 20,000 transfers per second); it keeps load below that ceiling and refuses the rest quickly
It doubles the database's capacity
It removes the need for a connection pool

questions.q: By Little's law, how many requests are in flight when 2,000 requests per second arrive and each takes 0.25 seconds?
questions.explain: In flight = arrival rate × time in the system = 2,000 × 0.25 = 500. If requests get slower, the number in flight grows, and so does memory use.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Three requests fill the window that ends at 1000 ms. At 1000 a new window starts with a fresh count of three. Six requests pass within about 100 ms, twice the limit: the boundary burst.
options: true true true false true true true false
true true true false false false false false
true true true true true true true true
true true true false true false false false

questions.q: The same traffic through a sliding log. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every request looks back 1000 ms from its own time. All eight arrive within 103 ms, so only the first three fit in any window.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two tokens allow a burst of two. After one second, one token is back. After four more seconds the bucket would hold four, but the capacity caps it at two.
options: yes yes no yes no yes yes no
yes yes no yes yes yes yes yes
yes yes no yes no yes no no
yes yes yes yes no yes yes no

questions.q: A bucket holds 0.5 tokens and refills 2 per second. A request costs 5 tokens. What does this print?
questions.explain: It needs 4.5 more tokens at 2 per second: 2.25 seconds. Retry-After is whole seconds, rounded up to 3.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: After a POST and two GETs, 3 tokens remain: not enough for another POST, which is refused without spending anything. The three cheap GETs then use the last 3 tokens.
options: POST:ok GET:ok GET:ok POST:429 GET:ok GET:ok GET:ok 0
POST:ok GET:ok GET:ok POST:ok GET:429 GET:429 GET:429 -2
POST:ok GET:ok GET:ok POST:429 GET:ok GET:ok GET:429 1
POST:ok GET:ok GET:ok POST:ok GET:ok GET:ok GET:ok 0

questions.q: An attacker sends 5 requests with made-up API keys, limited per key to 2. What does this print?
questions.explain: Every made-up key starts a fresh count, so all 5 pass. Counted by IP, the same 5 requests share one allowance. The map also grew by one entry per fake key, which is why unverified keys must never get their own buckets.

questions.q: What does this estimate print?
questions.explain: At the start of the window the whole previous window still counts. Halfway through, half of it does: 45 + 20 = 65. At 45 seconds, a quarter: 22.5 + 20 = 42.5.

questions.q: Two instances update a shared count with read-then-write. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both read 4, both decide 5 is within the limit, both write 5. Six requests were allowed but the counter says 5. An atomic increment returns 5 to one and 6 to the other.
options: 5 true
6 false
6 true
5 false

questions.q: What does this capacity check print?
questions.explain: 50 connections, each finishing a query every 4 ms, complete 12,500 queries per second at most. 7,500 requests per second have to be refused or queued, whatever the API code does.
options: 12500 refuse 7500/s
200 refuse 19800/s
12500 fits

questions.q: Write fixedWindow({ limit, windowMs }) returning (key, now) => decision, where a decision is { allowed: true, remaining } or { allowed: false, retryAfterMs } (time until the window ends). Keys are counted separately.
questions.explain: The window start comes from integer division of the time, so every instance computes the same window for the same moment. Bola's count is separate from Ada's, and at 1000 ms Ada is in a new window.

questions.q: Write tokenBucket({ capacity, refillPerSecond }) returning (key, now, cost = 1) => decision with lazy refill. Refused decisions include retryAfterMs (rounded up); allowed ones include remaining (rounded down).
questions.explain: A new bucket starts full, so a burst costing all 3 tokens passes. Then one token takes half a second to come back: refused with 500 ms, and at 250 ms there is half a token, so 250 ms more. After a long pause the bucket is capped at 3, not 19.

questions.q: Write slidingLog({ limit, windowMs }) returning (key, now) => decision. Keep, per key, the times of allowed requests in the last windowMs. A refused decision's retryAfterMs is when the oldest logged request leaves the window.
questions.explain: At 1000 ms both earlier requests are still within the last second, so the request is refused until 1900 ms, when the request from 900 ms drops out. The log has no window boundary to exploit.

questions.q: Write toResponse(decision) that turns a limiter decision into { status, headers }: allowed gives 200 with X-RateLimit-Remaining; refused gives 429 with Retry-After in whole seconds, rounded up, and at least 1.
questions.explain: Header values are strings. Rounding up, with a minimum of 1, means a client that obeys the header never comes back before the limiter can say yes.

questions.q: Write decide(request) that applies layered limits with the given allow(key, max) counter: first the IP ("ip:" + ip, max 5), then, if apiKey is not in validKeys, return "401" (the IP was already counted); then the key ("key:" + apiKey, max 2). Return "429 ip", "429 key" or "ok".
questions.explain: The guesses are refused as 401 but still count against their IP, so the sixth is stopped by the IP limit before the key is even checked. No counter was ever created for a made-up key.

questions.q: Simulate a shared store with an atomic incr(key) that adds one and returns the new value in one step. Write makeInstance(store, limit) returning (key) => boolean. Run 9 attempts over 3 instances (round robin) with a limit of 4 and print how many were allowed.
questions.explain: All instances share one count, and each increment returns a unique new value, so exactly 4 attempts get a number within the limit. This is what INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE … RETURNING or Redis INCR give you across servers.
